articles.text: Piedmont’s 55th annual July 4 parade was back in full swing Monday morning after a twoyear hiatus due to COVID. An estimated 2500 parade goers flooded Highland Avenue to see the parade, some sitting in chairs that were placed on the sidewalk as early as June 26. Piedmont’s own Uncle Sam, the celebrated artist Bruce Wolfe. Patti Edmonds’ bubble machine on the reviewing stand provided magic for paradegoers. Morning festivities began at 8 a.m. with the pre-parade pancake breakfast at Veterans Hall orchestrated by Piedmont Community Service Crew youth (see story on page 6). Diners enjoyed an al-fresco breakfast of sausages, fruit, pancakes, and coffee while being serenaded by the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band outside on the plaza. Floats and classic cars assembled at Highland and Park Way beginning at 10 a.m. City Council and school board members and other dignitaries climbed into their designated cars as the Zenith Parade Band practiced their first line tunes. Family photo opportunities were plentiful - the rainbow unicorn display at the Exedra, designed by the Piedmont Recreation Department, was a huge attraction, as was Smokey the Bear on one of the city’s fire engines. Piedmont Paramedic/Firefighter Matt Ziebarth went undercover as Smokey this year and took photos with many starstruck kids, who were then given tot-sized fire helmets by Fire Department staff. Piedmont Police officers were at each intersection along the route on Highland Avenue, greeting passersby and ensuring a safe event. Uncle Sam (Bruce Wolfe) and the Zenith band in the lead, Grand Marshal Dr. George Rutherford, Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration at UCSF, was driven in a 1960 Oldsmobile convertible. Rutherford was followed by Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, City Council members Jennifer Long, Conna McCarthy and Betsy Andersen, School Board members Veronica Thigpen, Megan Pillsbury, and Amal Smith, and new Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami. Making their first official appearance in the parade were Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales and family and Fire Chief Dave Brannigan with his wife and son. Youth Candy Ambassadors passed out sweet treats to kids and adults along the route. articles.text: Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. Honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic home/office/gym/classroom/ playground space where we do separate things next to one another – enhances learning and creativity benefits for both. According to Richard Louv, author of The Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. Since March, I have had the Dragon fun at Children’s Fairyland. benefit of looking out of my magical window to see this notion unfolding each day; children and adults reestablishing their connection to play, the outdoors, and one another after 15 months of keeping too much of their energy and toxic stress inside, both literally and figuratively. I watch children become swashbuckling mates on a pirate ship, play peekaboo with a donkey, climb on the back of the happy dragon, or catch bubbles blown by an elf. I also see their adults running behind them full of glee, smiles, relief, and a cup of coffee. Ever yone deser ves this moment to explore, imagine, create, play, scream, and run. Invest in restorative self-care for the whole family—get outside and play. Kymberly Miller is Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, located on the shores of Lake Merritt in the heart of Oakland, California. Since 1950.

articles.text: There will always be a need for people who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, the Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers and provide credit to students. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute is a community-based non-profit with over 120 members. Founded in 1992 by Dr. Richard Bailey, teams of volunteers remove 5,000 pounds of trash from Lake Merritt. Clean ups are held five times a week during the school year and three to four times a week in the summer. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue, next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help/ for more information and scheduling. Piedmont Community Service Crew Did you have pancakes at the pre-parade breakfast on Monday? Those flapjacks were prepared entirely by Piedmont Community Service Crew students. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a youth-led organization that accepts students age 14 through 21. Members are mostly from Piedmont High School, but all are welcome to join. Students get hands-on experience in many facets and work closely with Rebuilding Together Oakland and take the complete responsibility for the renovation of a low-income elderly person’s home. The group also does meal preparation and cooking at St. Mary’s Senior Center, Alameda County Community Food Bank, Dream Catcher Diner, and more. The crew was founded in 2004 by Piedmont resident Ken Li. Visit https://www.pcservicecrew. org/new-member to sign up. Running for a Better Oakland Running for a Better Oakland (RBO) strives to build a tolerant, healthy, and prosperous community - through running. The program teaches students how to build new relationships and self-esteem through the discipline and rigor of a structured race at Lake Merritt. Whether you’re a student, adult, runner or non-runner, all are welcome to volunteer. Meet-ups return in August, but you can sign up now to become a student’s “running buddy” or join the Green Team of high school volunteer and facilitate running games for kindergarten to fifth graders. RBO offers credit for volunteer hours. Visit https://www.rboakland. org/volunteer for more information. The MOSAIC project The MOSAIC project is a youth leadership project that provides extensive training in diversity and conflict-resolution for young adults and teens. Together, volunteers form a vibrant, cross-cultural community who serve as mentors for students in 4th and 5th grade who participate in Mosaic’s outdoor project. High school and college-aged volunteers are welcome to apply and are required to attend a weekend training retreat and volunteer for at least one session during the spring and fall. To apply, visit https://mosaicproject.org/ programs/youth-leadership-project/, or contact Youth Leadership Director Khemnes Fisher at 510- 452-3377 or email at khemnes@ mosaicproject.org. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. pages.text: Wednesday, July 6, 2022 9 Volunteer opportunities open to Piedmonters By Allyson Aleksey There will always be a need for people who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, the Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers and provide credit to students. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute is a community-based non-profit with over 120 members. Founded in 1992 by Dr. Richard Bailey, teams of volunteers remove 5,000 pounds of trash from Lake Merritt. Clean ups are held five times a week during the school year and three to four times a week in the summer. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue, next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help/ for more information and scheduling. Piedmont Community Service Crew Did you have pancakes at the pre-parade breakfast on Monday? Those flapjacks were prepared entirely by Piedmont Community Service Crew students. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a youth-led organization that accepts students age 14 through 21. Members are mostly from Piedmont High School, but all are welcome to join. Students get hands-on experience in many facets and work closely with Rebuilding Together Oakland and take the complete responsibility for the renovation of a low-income elderly person’s home. The group also does meal preparation and cooking at St. Mary’s Senior Center, Alameda County Community Food Bank, Dream Catcher Diner, and more. The crew was founded in 2004 by Piedmont resident Ken Li. Visit https://www.pcservicecrew. org/new-member to sign up. Running for a Better Oakland Running for a Better Oakland (RBO) strives to build a tolerant, healthy, and prosperous community - through running. The program teaches students how to build new relationships and self-esteem through the discipline and rigor of a structured race at Lake Merritt. Whether you’re a student, adult, runner or non-runner, all are welcome to volunteer. Meet-ups return in August, but you can sign up now to become a student’s “running buddy” or join the Green Team of high school volunteer and facilitate running games for kindergarten to fifth graders. RBO offers credit for volunteer hours. Visit https://www.rboakland. org/volunteer for more information. The MOSAIC project The MOSAIC project is a youth leadership project that provides extensive training in diversity and conflict-resolution for young adults and teens. Together, volunteers form a vibrant, cross-cultural community who serve as mentors for students in 4th and 5th grade who participate in Mosaic’s outdoor project. High school and college-aged volunteers are welcome to apply and are required to attend a weekend training retreat and volunteer for at least one session during the spring and fall. To apply, visit https://mosaicproject.org/ programs/youth-leadership-project/, or contact Youth Leadership Director Khemnes Fisher at 510- 452-3377 or email at khemnes@ mosaicproject.org. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. Visit https:// mercybrownbag.org/volunteer/ to sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Email suggestions to Allyson Aleksey at Allysonaaleksey@gmail.com. articles.text: Rafaella Gomes graduated from Piedmont High in 2021 and competes year-round on UC San Diego’s fencing program and with the Brazilian National Team. She recently competed with Brazil at the 2022 Pan American Fencing Championships from June 2-8 in Asunción, Paraguay, finishing 16th of 44 in the Foil Women’s Senior Individual category. She helped Brazil finish fourth of 10 teams and was the youngest competitor in her group, the result helped qualify her country for the 2023 event. She is now in the midst of training for the prestigious 2022 Senior World Championships in Cairo, Egypt on July 15-23. “When I am not competing for UC San Diego in the NCAA circuit, I am competing in the Brazilian national circuit, representing Brazil at international tournaments throughout the year. I tested positive for COVID following the event but was lucky enough to avoid the most serious condition. Now, I am back at practice with the Senior World Championships right around the corner,” said Gomes. Gomes continues to train with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, which is run by the Photos courtesy of cbesgrima.org.br Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, competes internationally with the Brazil National Team. She’s pictured here after winning Bronze at the 2022 Junior Pan American Championship. U.S. Men’s Foil Fencing Team coach Greg Massialas and routinely produces Olympic talent. She trained with the foundation for eight years prior to starting her collegiate fencing career. Rafaella Gomes reached the NCAA Championships with UC San Diego and is currently the world’s No. 100 ranked fencer in the senior category. Rafaella lets out an exuberant yell at the Senior Pan American Championship. She placed 16th overall and helped Brazil finish fourth. “I am far from where I want to be with my fencing, so I am in an intensive training program. I have practice at the Massialas Foundation every weekday and Saturdays for two hours. Practices includes 30 minutes of intense, fencing-specific footwork drills, an hour of fencing, and 30 minutes of one-on-one work with a coach,” described Gomes. As for her collegiate career at UC San Diego, Gomes had a remarkable freshman year. She reached the NCAA National Championship on March 27, and qualified for the prestigious tournament after taking silver at the NCAA West Regional Championship on March 12. She also finished second in the Mountain Pacific Sports Federation Fencing Championships’ Women’s Foil on March 13 and earned the MPSF Newcomer of the Year award. She said that her results at the NCAA Championship only fuels her fire after competing on short-rest from the Junior Pan American Championships shortly before. “I loved my first year in the NCAA. Next year, my goal is to qualify for NCAA Nationals again and place in the top 16. I arrived at the competition at 1 a.m. the morning of the tournament directly from the Junior Pan American Championships and was unable to perform my best. One of the biggest challenges I have faced is juggling a rigorous academic workload along with three independent competition circuits,” explained Gomes. Gomes is currently ranked No. 49 in the world’s junior category after taking bronze at the Junior Pan American Championship last March. She’s currently No. 100 globally in the senior category and has the third-highest senior ranking for the Brazil National Team. Look for more coverage of Rafaella following the 2022 Senior World Championship tournament in Cairo.

Nearing the completing of the first week of the 2022 Tour de France, the peloton is ascending into hills and mountains for the next eight stages. Belgium’s Wout van Aert of Jumbo-Visma currently leads the General Classification standings after placing second in the first three stages and an impressive win on Tuesday’s hill ride. It has been a strong first week for the Jumbo-Visma team with three of its riders in the top seven. Van Aert is considered one of the strongest sprinters in cycling but is usually slotted in as the team’s third rider behind Primož Roglič and Jonas Vingegaard, who are currently in sixth and seventh. Back-to-back defending champion Tadej Pogačar is in third, 32 seconds back of van Aert and seven back of second-place Yves Lampart, who is also from Belgium. The next week of riding could provide dramatic changes to the general classification standing. Wednesday, July 6, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. KAI JOHNSON Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Weber State Class of 2025 Kai Johnson was a four-year starter at Piedmont High and recently completed her freshman year at Weber State. She appeared in 26 games last season, with 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one block. At Piedmont, she burst on the scene in 2017 and was the team captain for her final two years at the school. She was named nu the Post as 2021 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. She earned first-team All-League honors as a junior and senior a PHS. Johnson was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball program, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. What is your workout program this summer? On Mondays, I lift from 7:45- 8:30 a.m. followed by practice from 9-11:30 a.m. and individual training workout. Tuesdays, I have practices from 9-11:30 a.m. On Wednesdays I work in the gym and shoot during the day. Thursday, I lift from 7:45-8:30 a.m., practice, and then have a group workout. Friday includes practice from 9:30-11 a.m., lift from 11:30-12:45 p.m. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My one and only goal for my fitness is to get to a point where I can consistently keep running without getting tired, which is both physical and mental. How are you measuring your development? My development is measured through how I’m producing in practice. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m training by myself, with teammates, and coaches at school. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? A milestone is being able communicate effectively on the court while being tired. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? I would say work for what you want, because nothing is handed to you in sports at the collegiate level. You have to not only compete with yourself, but also with your teammates because you want a spot on the court. You have to work for the things you want, no matter if you’re a freshman, because that spot isn’t guaranteed. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Photo courtesy of WeberStateSports.com Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, just finished her freshman year at Weber State. Piedmont High Class of 2024 Natalia Martinez is entering her junior year at Piedmont High and was recently named the 2022 Sophomore of the Year by the Post. Her team went 24-7 last season and made the North Coast Section finals, where they were seeded #2. They lost to No. 1 Marin Catholic in the finals but qualified for their first CIF State Tournament in 11 years. Martinez scored 31 points in the second round of the State tourney in a game Piedmont lost by 7 points to No. 8 Lincoln. She earned first-team AllLeague honors and scored 19 points in the NCS Finals, while scoring 14 points in the second half. Martinez also exploded for 33 points in the NCS quarterfinals against St. Mary’s and 27 in the opening round with Swett. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program is to get my shots up when I wake up, usually about 5 am. Later on, I go to my team practice/workouts, whether it is high school or AAU. In the evening, I do some individual cardio, strength training, and stretching. What are your fitness goals for the summer? One of my fitness goals is to gain strength in my upper and lower body. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by setting deadlines and by tracking milestones. For example, one of my deadlines was to squat 120 before June 20th, and as of right now, I’m squatting 120 clean with no struggle. Staff Photo Natalia Martinez was the Post’s 2022 Sophomore of the Year and Freshman of the Year one year earlier. She enters a big junior season this winter. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I do workouts by myself all the time. I still work with my coaches in the offseason to get sharper, and I also work my trainer from Fit Evolution for lifting and conditioning. I would advise younger athletes to practice good fundamentals all the time in whatever sport you play, and don’t cut corners. Everyone has the same 24 hours and every day that passes is a chance for you to get better. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A milestone I recently achieved was receiving my first college scholarship offer. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? articles.text: With summer here, the Class of 2023 looks to next school year as a time that could be a defining year of their sports careers. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons ahead. WILSON WONG Volleyball Wilson Wong has been the volleyball team captain since his sophomore year, when the program began after an absence of 20 years. Last spring, Wong helped lead the team to qualify for the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs for the first time since 1999. Staff Photo Wilson Wong will be entering his third year as captain of the volleyball team. In the playoffs, Piedmont received the No. 11 seed and upset No. 6 Analy High School on the road in Sebastopol 3-2 on May 3. Wong was instrumental in Piedmont’s first-round win over Analy with five kills and six aces. Their trip in the playoffs ended with a 3-1 loss to Archie Williams in San Anselmo on May 5. The bulk of the Highlanders’ lineup from last season will be returning next spring, including Wong, John Champion, Kai Lambert, Owen Kelly, Brayden Day, Eric Olaru-Hagen, James MaNguyen, and Shunji Higashi. MOLLY ASHTON Lacrosse Photo by Todd Marshburn Molly Ashton earned an All-League selection last spring and will be a key player on the lacrosse team next spring. Molly Ashton earned an honorable mention for All-League honors last season after helping the lacrosse team go 4-1 in league (9-10 overall). PHS lost in the first-round of the NCS playoffs, but Ashton emerged as a key player in coach Carlton Chan’s system. She scored three goas last season against Dougherty Valley on March 11 and Tamalpais on April 4. Her classmates for next year include Elizabeth Weisbrock, Sofia Johnson, and Holland Feinberg. T.J. O’NEIL Soccer Staff Photo T.J. O’Neil earned a first-team All-League selection on Piedmont’s North Coast Section championship soccer team. T.J. O’Neil earned a first-team All-League selection as a key midfielder on coach Todd Sullivan’s league and North Coast Section championship team. The Highlanders went 15-2-4 overall last season on its way to their second consecutive WACC Shoreline title and being undefeated in league play at 10-0-0. It would have been their thirdstraight banner after going undefeated in the shortened 2021 pandemic year, but no league titles were awarded. Piedmont captured the school’s first-ever Division 4 North Coast Section title and received the No. 1 seed for the first time. It defeated University 1-0 to claim the championship. The Highlanders accomplished another first in its school history by reaching the CIF State Tournament as the No. 6 seed before losing 2-0 to No. 3 Sacred Heart Prep. In the NCS title game, O’Neil frequently disrupted University’s attack and moved the ball fluidly when in possession, nearly scoring in the 24th minute of action.

articles.text: Photos courtesy of McDonald’s official Instagram Mackie McDonald improved his world ranking five spots to No. 50 on the ATP ladder. Former Piedmont tennis star Mackie McDonald saw his trip to Wimbledon come to an end in the second round on Thursday, June 30, losing to Richard Gasquet of France in four sets, 6-3, 3-6, 6-4, 6-3. Despite the result, he improved his ATP World Ranking five positions to No. 50, one shy of his career high. Against Gasquet, who entered with the No. 69 world rank, McDonald was inconsistent while serving with 10 aces but committed eight double faults. He hit more winners than Gasquet (66), but committed 52 unforced errors compared to the Frenchman’s 27 – the clear difference in the match. McDonald had several opportunities in break points against Gasquet as the returner on serves but was only able to convert three of 16 attempts. He missed three break points in the last set, which he lost 6-3. Gasquet took his fifth and sixth-game match winner after McDonald held a break point opportunity in both games. The trail is a gorgeous walk under a canopy of Redwood trees, California Bay Laurel and Oak trees. The creek is mostly dry, but still has some good resting points. Walking for 1.2 miles, the path intersects with Central Park Drive, which leads to a bustling parking lot for Tilden’s Little Farm – a popular location for kids. After 0.4 of a mile, the parking lot becomes the Wildcat Creek trail. You’ll only be spending a brief time on the path, turning left after 0.2 of a mile towards the walkway leading to Jewel Lake. In addition to some close exposures to your barnyard friends, the path gives some great views of the Berkeley hills. The majority on the Wildcat Gorge and Wildcat Creek trails. articles.text: Museum to celebrate opening of Diego Rivera’s America San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is celebrating the opening of an exhibit titled Diego Rivera’s America with a free day of community activities and art on Sunday, July 17 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Diego Rivera’s America is an in-depth examination of the artist’s work and brings together more than 150 of Rivera’s paintings and drawings. articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Bejing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei?utm_medium=email&utm_source=famsfmktg&utm_campaign=guopei&utm_content=consideration_20220408&mc_cid=e- 25a62443e&mc_eid=573801a180 to obtain tickets. articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert celebrating composer Harry Warren this Sunday, July 10. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of the most successful film composers; Warren has composed music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and piaIn the Tradition Piano Trio nist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at https://bpt.me/5316993 or at the door. San Francisco Symphony shown performing at Stern Grove in 2013. The Symphony is a regular headliner of the summer music festival.

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony will close out this month’s performances at Stern Grove Festival, a series of free music festivals at an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The program includes music by Nicolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Sergei Prokofiev, Dinuk Wijeratne, Johannes Brahms, and Igor Stravinsky. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization that presents free music festivals in the city since its inception in 1938. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. articles.text: A scene from the Coen brother’s movie, A Serious Man. Review by Chris Honoré Known for their original sometimes off-center films, the prolific Coen Brothers have been at work refining and expanding their craft since 1991. During that time, they’ve garnered eight Academy Award nominations, and won three Oscars for No Country for Old Men. Their films are wide ranging, from comedies to thrillers, some unflinchingly violent while others meld various genres. They’re also known for boxing the compass regarding settings: O Brother Where Art Thou? was set in the South during the Great Depression; Fargo in the Dakotas; No Country for Old Men in the Southwest; The Big Lebowski on the West Coast; and Burn After Reading in D.C. Of all their films, A Serious Man, released in 2009, may be their most contemplative if not their most personal. It focuses on Larry Gopnik (Michael Stuhlberg), a physics professor, married, two children and a man about to experience a major existential crisis. Like dominos falling, he is suddenly faced with a series of unexpected developments: his wife, Judith (Sari Lennick), announces she has fallen in love with Sy Ableman (Fred Melamed) and wants a divorce; his neighbor, an anti-Semite, is encroaching on his yard; his much anticipated tenure seems in jeopardy; his son, on the cusp of his bar mitzvah, is a pothead; his daughter wants a nose-job; and his brother, Arthur (Richard Kind), is sleeping on the sofa and prone to crying jags when he’s not up late at night, lancing a boil on his neck. Though the cultural context is a Midwestern Jewish community in 1967, Larry’s abiding angst is strikingly universal. His life is out of control. Perpetually perplexed, Larry tries to cope and keep up, but he can’t summon the will to strongly react. He is drowning in reasonableness as his life slips into a grim comedy of errors, as if the universe is conspiring against him. And though he never laughs, or even smiles, clearly the Coens believe that humor may be, at least for the audience, the only refuge. A Serious Man is a character study that frustrates and infuriates and happily entertains. Life sorts itself out and that pervasive sense of perplexed despair eventually morphs into something more positive, more manageable. It just requires a bit of tenacity – being tenaciously reasonable. A Serious Man. Written and Directed by Joel and Ethan Coen. Starring Michael Stuhlbarg, Fred Melamed, Jessica McManos, Richard Kind, Adam Arkin, Sari Lennick and Aaron Wolff. 1 hr. 45 min. Rated R. Released in theaters in 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The iconic fantasy adventure Peter Pan, a timeless allegory, was co-written by director P.J. Hogan. It’s a live-action film based on J.M. Barrie’s 1911 novel, and, when fully titled, is referred to as The Boy Who Wouldn’t Grow Up. It was released into theaters in 2003 and is now streaming. This incarnation, with a darker, edgier tone stars Jeremy Sumpter as cocky, self-confident Peter, who is not only an American actor but also male, as opposed to the fact that the character Peter Pan of the past has always been played by pixie-like women (think Mary Martin). The story begins in an Edwardian London nursery where teen Wendy Darling (Rachel Hurd Wood) is telling a riveting story to her younger brothers John (Harry Newell) and Michael (Freddie Poppelwell). Meanwhile, Peter Pan is listening to Wendy’s tale just outside the nursery window, intrigued by her narrative and ability to create a mesmerizing tale. The adventure begins when Peter, with the help of the magical fairy dust of the astonishing Tinker Bell (Ludville Sagnier), invites the children to fly with him to Neverland where Wendy can meet the Lost Boys and tell them her stories. She soon becomes a surrogate mother to the remarkable clan. This version of Peter Pan makes a valiant attempt to remain true to Barrie’s original story. There is, naturally, the often nefarious, scary, flying Captain Hook (John Isaac) who has the ability to change his missing arm (bitten off by an alligator) as he pleases. Meanwhile Wendy’s mother, Mrs. Darling (Olivia Williams) is at home worried about her missing children. The Lost Boys are continually intriguing, and Hook’s pirate ship is wonderful. As is Tinker Bell, nicknamed Tink by Peter. And let’s not forget the confrontation between Wendy, on the verge of womanhood, and Peter who makes it clear to her that he wishes never to grow up. Their budding romance, however, is ever present. The film is filled with scary moments, lots of action, sword fights, amazing flights across the sky, and the remarkable Asiatic mermaids who emerge from the Neverland lagoon. This version of Peter Pan is a magical adventure that will capture tweens and teens, as if pixie dust had been sprinkled on every scene. Peter Pan. Directed by P.J. Hogan. Live-action adventure, fantasy. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released into theaters in 2003. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Jeremy Sumpter as Peter Pan.

The story begins in an Edwardian London nursery where teen Wendy Darling (Rachel Hurd Wood) is telling a riveting story to her younger brothers John (Harry Newell) and Michael (Freddie Poppelwell). Meanwhile, Peter Pan is listening to Wendy’s tale just outside the nursery window, intrigued by her narrative and ability to create a mesmerizing tale. The adventure begins when Peter, with the help of the magical fairy dust of the astonishing Tinker Bell (Ludville Sagnier), invites the children to fly with him to Neverland where Wendy can meet the Lost Boys and tell them her stories. She soon becomes a surrogate mother to the remarkable clan. This version of Peter Pan makes a valiant attempt to remain true to Barrie’s original story. There is, naturally, the often nefarious, scary, flying Captain Hook (John Isaac) who has the ability to change his missing arm (bitten off by an alligator) as he pleases. Meanwhile Wendy’s mother, Mrs. Darling (Olivia Williams) is at home worried about her missing children. The Lost Boys are continually intriguing, and Hook’s pirate ship is wonderful. As is Tinker Bell, nicknamed Tink by Peter. And let’s not forget the confrontation between Wendy, on the verge of womanhood, and Peter who makes it clear to her that he wishes never to grow up. Their budding romance, however, is ever present. The film is filled with scary moments, lots of action, sword fights, amazing flights across the sky, and the remarkable Asiatic mermaids who emerge from the Neverland lagoon. This version of Peter Pan is a magical adventure that will capture tweens and teens, as if pixie dust had been sprinkled on every scene. Peter Pan. Directed by P.J. Hogan. The route of the No. 12 line in Piedmont was selected as the morning’s destination on June 29. Before starting off, a short review of the Key System was provided as a refresher for those on the previous walk, and an introduction for those who hadn’t been on it. In the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay population grew in the late 1800’s, developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established The Realty Syndicate. This company acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay for homes. Potential buyers needed transportation to get from their new homes to work in the area and in San Francisco. The Key System was conceived by Borax Smith as a way to sell The Realty Syndicate’s land. The Key System began service in 1903 in Berkeley, and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. Some background information on the No. 12 Line was also shared before the group started off. It was originally called the “Grand Avenue & Hollis Street Line.” At its fullest, this line went along Oakland, Fairview, Grand, Webster, 14th, Market, 24th, Adeline, 32nd, Hollis, to Yerba Buena. The Grand Avenue & Hollis Street line began as a shuttle on Grand Avenue from Wildwood Avenue, at the city limits, to Perry Street near where Oakland Avenue and the MacArthur Freeway are today. The line connected there with cars of the Lakeshore Avenue line. In 1915 the end of the line was extended from Grand Avenue up Fairview Avenue. The route had a few name changes over the years, but in 1928 its name was finalized as the “No. 12” line.” However, on June 27, 1948 the No. 12 Grand Avenue streetcar service was abandoned, and buses replaced the service. The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, then down Jerome Avenue on their way to Fairview. They couldn’t pass up the opportunity to walk up the charming, short Keefer Court cul-de-sac. This street has a home at its end with a marvelous, cactus garden front yard that is a delight to see. Other homes have a similar look. Long-time walkers remembered stories of how the homeowner transformed his garden to the marvel that it is today from what was an ordinary yard. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received reviews from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indie-next-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. July #1 Pick “Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow” is the beginning of one Shakespeare’s most famous soliloquies in Macbeth. It is also the title of author Gabrielle Zevin’s novel on friendship, love, and video games. Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow By Gabrielle Zevin, Knopf, Fiction “I am deeply mourning finishing this book. Zevin has masterfully created a love story for friendship that will stay with me. While the characters were imperfect and strikingly human, following this span of 30 years left me wanting more.” —Vina Castillo, Kew & Willow Books, Kew Gardens, NY A Prayer for the Crown-Shy: A Monk and Robot Book By Becky Chambers, Tordotcom, Science Fiction “Just as wonderful and as tender as A Psalm for the Wild-Built. A sweet and earthy cup of tea to warm the soul. New and old characters to giggle with, cry with, and just flat out fall in love with. A book that I will return to again and again.” —Allie Bisset, Third Street Books, McMinnville, OR Fellowship Point By Alice Elliott Dark, Scribner/Marysue Rucci Books, Fiction “Fellowship Point was a joy to read. Alice Elliott Dark has crafted unforgettable characters in a sweeping story of friendship, family, and life as a whole. I hit pause on the real world for a bit and fell deeply in love with this gem of a novel.” —Kaitlin Smith, Copperfield’s Books, Healdsburg, CA Lapvona By Ottessa Moshfegh, Penguin Press, Fiction “Lapvona is a truly marvelous Indie Next Best Reads of July and original creation that walks the iconic Moshfegh line of stomach churning and profound. This book has its underbelly exposed and its eyes to the heavens.” —Ellie Eaton, Busboys and Poets, Washington, DC Juniper & Thorn By Ava Reid, Harper Voyager, Fantasy “A gorgeous story influenced by one of the Brothers Grimm’s darkest tales. At the center, two souls find a haven in each other while escaping evil worse than any monster under the bed. Juniper & Thorn is bewitching and utterly captivating.” —Tarah Jennings, Mitzi’s Books, Rapid City, SD ways. Talty’s characters live and breathe on the page. This book is a celebration of life and language.” —Margaret Leonard, Dotters Books, Eau Claire, WI The Mermaid of Black Conch By Monique Roffey, Knopf, Fiction “Tragedy displaces pain after a curse born of a thousand-year old jealousy exiles the beautiful Aycayia to a life in the sea. The Mermaid of Black Conch is a modern-day embodiment of our longing for community. Ruthless and beautiful.” —Kayleen Rohrer, InkLink Books, East Troy, WI Elsewhere By Alexis Schaitkin, Celadon Books, Fiction “Timeless! Beautifully haunting! All of the comparisons are apt — this is a modern day The Lottery penned in gorgeous prose, with an underlying mystery that is a thrill to untangle.” —Chelsea Berry, Bull Moose, Portland, ME Also a Poet: Frank O’Hara, My Father, and Me By Ada Calhoun, Grove Press, Biography “Ada Calhoun has given us a poised, magnificent memoir on family, her father, and of huge emotional and personal exploration. She delivers an unveiled perspective on capital ‘L’ literary New York. This one shines brilliantly for all to see.” —Scott Abel, Solid State Books, Washington, DC One’s Company By Ashley Hutson, W. W. Norton & Company, Fiction “Where do I even begin? An original and poignant story of obsession, trauma and the desire to escape into another reality as a means of survival. This is one of the most bonkers books I’ve ever read, and one of my favorite books of 2022.” —Gaël LeLamer, Books & Books, Coral Gables, FL What Moves the Dead By T. Kingfisher, Tor Nightfire, Horror “Rarely do I come across horror novels with such witty and delightful characters. The dialogue made me want to sit down to tea with each person, but the creepy gothic atmosphere made me want to forgo the tea and run away screaming instead.” —Anna Hersh, Wild Rumpus, Minneapolis, MN Life Ceremony By Sayaka Murata, Ginny Tapley Takemori (Transl.), Grove Press, Short Stories “Think Kelly Link, Ottessa Moshfegh, and a pinch of surrealism. Weird and absolutely delightful!” —Rachel Brewer, Carmichael’s Bookstore, Louisville, KY The It Girl By Ruth Ware, Gallery/Scout Press, Thriller “This is the perfect summer read, it grabs you from the first few pages and engrosses you in its murder mystery. Sweet, heartbreaking, and completely original, this novel by Katie Hafner is wholly unforgettable.” —Mary O’Malley, Skylark Bookshop, Columbia, MO Our Wives Under the Sea By Julia Armfield, Flatiron Books, Fiction “A haunting meditation on relationships in all their messy glory. The descriptive language is beautiful and unforgettable. I’ll be thinking about this one for a while.” —David Vogel, Literati Bookstore, Ann Arbor, MI The Dead Romantics By Ashley Poston, Berkley, Romance “I never thought I’d gush over a romance set in a funeral home featuring a ghost. Yes, please! I adored the premise of this story and the characters were so lovable and fun. Highly enjoyed it and will be talking about it nonstop!” —Jen Miller, Old Town Books, Alexandria, VA The Lies I Tell By Julie Clark, Sourcebooks Landmark, Thriller “Kat Roberts has waited a decade to expose con artist Meg Williams. This is definitely not one to miss!” —Rebecca Minnock, Murder By the Book, Houston, TX Grown Ups By Marie Aubert, Rosie Hedger (Transl.), Pushkin Press, Fiction “I was hooked from the first line of Grown Ups, a wickedly fun novel about people behaving badly: ‘Other people’s children, always, everywhere.’ Sibling rivalry, midlife crises, and unease play out in this delicious train wreck of a book.” —Jhoanna Belfer, Bel Canto Books, Long Beach, CA Jackie & Me By Louis Bayard, Algonquin Books, Historical Fiction “Lem Billings befriends Jackie Bouvier as she is sized up by the Kennedy family to become the wife of the up-and-coming politician. Told by an older Lem, it’s an insightful story of friendship, love, and sacrifice. Book clubs will love it!” —Beth Carpenter, The Country Bookshop, Southern Pines, NC The Angel of Rome By Jess Walter, Harper, Short Stories “The first sentences in this astonishing collection dare you not to read further. Walter exposes his characters for what they are in subtle and startling PAPERBACK RECOMMENDATIONS Appleseed By Matt Bell, Mariner Books, Fiction “This cross between a Shakespeare drama and a Grimm fairy tale is unsettling, attention-grabbing, and thought-provoking in the way stories do so well when reason often fails. A powerful read!” —Helen Eddy, The Book Shoppe, Boone, IA Filthy Animals By Brandon Taylor, Riverhead Books, Short Stories “These stories about human relationships range from those between lovers, friends, and family. How is it that Taylor can write so that we can see the interior crevices of these characters’ souls?” —Rachel Watkins, Avid Bookshop, Athens, GA How to Catch a Mole: Wisdom from a Life Lived in Nature By Marc Hamer, Greystone Books, Essays “Sublimely touching, this book has a balance that makes for good nature writing. Hamer’s memoir waxes and wanes, at times gruesome, sensual, violent, and awestruck. A book for fans of the way Mary Oliver lived and talked about her life.” —Afton Montgomery, Tattered Cover Book Store, Denver, CO The Inheritance of Orquídea Divina By Zoraida Córdova, Atria Books, Fiction “This story sparkles and enchants! It’s a rich and layered multigeneration saga featuring strong women and a mystery veiled in magical realism that will tease and feed your imagination.” —Grace Rajendran, University Book Store, Seattle, WA Island Queen By Vanessa Riley, William Morrow Paperbacks, Fiction “Both sweeping and intimate, beautiful and painful, this novel based on the life of Dorothy Kirwan Thomas is exquisite. Riley’s research is in the detail of each chapter, and readers will find themselves compulsively turning the pages.” —Destinee Hodge, East City Bookshop, Washington, DC Lightning Strike By William Kent Krueger, Atria Books, Mystery “In this prequel to the Cork O’Connor series set in 1963, we meet 12-year-old Cork’s family as his father investigates a murder. Even as Cork believes he will never be a cop, we can see Cork’s inevitable future as an investigator.” —Carol Blizzard Dunn, Northwind Book & Fiber, Spooner, WI

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost-making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials then can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. More information can be found at the City’s news and notifications page. Contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov or (510) 420-3058 if you have any questions. articles.text: The popular Dress Best for Less bag sale continues at the same location on the last Saturday of the month. From 10 a.m. to noon residents can fill a paper grocery bag with items like clothing, toys, and books for $10 at the Marking Room, 799 Magnolia Avenue. Founded in 1982 by Piedmont resident Wendy Willrich and a group of Havens School moms, Dress Best is a way to collect unneeded household items and clothing to sell to the community to raise money for the school district. They were given an unused room at Havens School, but quickly outgrew the space and rented a storefront on Piedmont Avenue, their original retail location. DBFL donates most of its profits to the Piedmont Education Foundation, a non-profit that raises money for Piedmont schools. DBFL has donated more than $1 million since its inception. Donations that cannot be sold in the store are donated to other non-profits. The store gives back to the broader community by donating to St. Vincent de Paul, Children’s Hospital, and animal rescue organizations in the East Bay. More than half of clothing donations received by DBFL are donated to St. Vincent de Paul, helping families in need in Alameda County through gifts made directly to them or through proceeds made from the store. These proceeds allow the organization to provide food, rent, job training and other services to those in need. DBFL also donates children’s items to Love Twice, a non-profit organization that provides newborns in need with quality baby clothing for the first year of life. Donations of gently used, high Dress Best Marking room is located at 799 Magnolia Avenue. quality clothing and home goods are welcome, and all donations are tax deductible. The retail store is at 4020 Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. Store hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. DBFL’s marking room for sales and donations is by appointment only. Visit http://dressbestforless.org/donate/ to make an appointment.
